questions.prompt: **Beacon frames**: who sends them, and what are the TWO most important pieces of information inside?
options: The AP sends them periodically to all hosts in range; they carry the AP's SSID and MAC address
Hosts send them to discover APs; they carry the host's IP and MAC
The router sends them; they carry the subnet mask and gateway
The AP sends them only on request; they carry the WiFi password
questions.explain: Beacons are sent **by the Access Point**, periodically, broadcast to all wireless hosts in range. Contents to quote: **the AP's name (SSID)** and **the AP's MAC address**.

questions.prompt: The TWO ways a wireless device can find/connect to an Access Point are:
options: Passive scanning (listen for beacons) and active scanning (broadcast a Probe Request; APs answer)
DHCP scanning and ARP scanning
Polling and token passing
RTS scanning and CTS scanning
questions.explain: **Passive**: host listens for beacon frames. **Active**: host broadcasts a **Probe Request**; APs reply with Probe Responses. Then the host selects an AP and associates.

questions.source: Drill P1(d) — 1819 real (4 steps to an IP)
questions.prompt: Order the FOUR steps from a host arriving in a WLAN until it can use an IP address:
items: Scan channels / listen for beacons (or send Probe Request) → discover APs
Select an AP and send an Association Request
AP replies with an Association Response (host associated)
Run DHCP (discover-offer-request-ACK) to obtain an IP in the AP's subnet
questions.explain: Scan → Association Request → Association Response → **DHCP**. The association gives link-layer connectivity; DHCP gives the network-layer address. Both halves are needed for the full 4 marks.

questions.prompt: A and C both transmit to B; A and C are out of each other's range. The **hidden terminal problem** means:
options: A and C cannot hear each other, so they transmit simultaneously and collide AT B — and neither can detect it
B hides its MAC from A and C
A's signal is encrypted so C cannot read it
B refuses frames from two senders
questions.explain: **Hidden terminal:** A↔B fine, C↔B fine, but A and C can't sense each other (range/obstacle) → simultaneous transmissions **interfere at B**, undetectable at the senders. **Fading** is the signal-strength twin: A and C are too attenuated at each other's location to sense one another, yet both still strong at B. Sketch: two overlapping circles around A and C, B in the overlap.

questions.prompt: Which MAC protocol suits this wireless network, and why not CSMA/CD?
options: CSMA/CA — a wireless sender cannot detect collisions (own signal overwhelms reception; hidden terminals)
CSMA/CD — collision detection is faster
Token ring — guarantees fairness
Pure ALOHA — simplest
questions.explain: **CSMA/CA (IEEE 802.11 MAC)**. CD is unsuitable: while transmitting, the sender's own signal drowns the weak received signal, and hidden terminals make some collisions physically undetectable at the sender — so 802.11 **avoids** collisions instead of detecting them.

items: Channel idle for DIFS → transmit the ENTIRE frame (no collision detection)
If busy → pick a random backoff; the timer counts down ONLY while idle (freezes when busy)
Transmit when the backoff timer reaches 0
If no ACK arrives → increase the backoff interval and repeat
questions.explain:
Sender: DIFS-idle → send; busy → backoff counting only during idle; timer 0 → send; **no ACK → loss assumed → bigger backoff, retry**.
Receiver: frame OK → **ACK after SIFS** (ACKs exist precisely because of hidden terminals).

questions.prompt: How does the **RTS/CTS** exchange prevent collisions of long data frames?
options: The CTS from the AP is heard by ALL stations — only the named sender transmits; others defer; collisions can only hit the tiny RTS packets
RTS encrypts the channel until the data is sent
CTS doubles the transmission power of the sender
RTS reserves a separate frequency band
questions.explain: Sender → short **Request-To-Send**; AP → **Clear-To-Send**, heard by everyone: the named station sends its long frame, all others stay silent. If two RTS collide, only tiny packets are lost (cheap). **Long data frames never collide** — the channel is reserved by small packets.

questions.prompt: H1 (wireless) sends to the Internet via AP and router R1. The 802.11 frame's addresses are:
options: A1 = AP's MAC (receiver of this transmission), A2 = H1's MAC (transmitter), A3 = R1's MAC (wired-side anchor)
A1 = R1, A2 = AP, A3 = H1
A1 = H1, A2 = AP, A3 = R1
A1 = AP, A2 = R1, A3 = H1
questions.explain:
Rules: **A1 = receiver of this wireless transmission (AP)**, **A2 = transmitter (H1)**, **A3 = the off-cell node on the wired side (R1's interface)**. (A4 only in ad-hoc mode.)
**Why three?** The AP is a link-layer relay between TWO links (wireless cell + wired LAN); Ethernet's two addresses describe only one link, so the frame must also carry the router's MAC for the AP to bridge correctly.

questions.prompt: Mobile A: permanent address **128.119.40.186** (home), care-of address **79.129.13.2** (visited). Which is correct?
options: Correspondents always use the permanent address; the HOME AGENT uses the care-of address to tunnel datagrams to A's location
Correspondents must learn the care-of address before sending anything
The permanent address changes every move; the COA is fixed
Both addresses are assigned by the visited network
questions.explain: **Permanent address**: in the home network, never changes — what the **correspondent always uses**. **Care-of address**: temporary, in the visited network — **used by the home agent** to tunnel datagrams to A's current location.

questions.prompt: Order the **indirect routing** steps when correspondent B sends to mobile A (visiting a foreign network):
items: B sends the datagram to A's PERMANENT address → routed to A's home network
The HOME AGENT intercepts, encapsulates it in a new datagram addressed to the CARE-OF address, and tunnels it
The FOREIGN AGENT decapsulates and delivers the original datagram to A
A replies DIRECTLY to B via ordinary IP routing
questions.explain:
Indirect routing = **triangle**: B → home network → (tunnel) → foreign agent → A; reply goes direct.
**Triangle routing problem**: every packet detours via the home network — worst when B and A sit in the SAME visited network.
**Direct routing fix**: B queries the home agent ONCE for the COA, then sends straight to the foreign agent. Costs: non-transparent to B, and if A moves again the first ('anchor') foreign agent must chain-forward.

questions.prompt: In 3G, a user's **data** (Internet) traffic follows which chain after the radio leg (mobile → Node B → RNC)?
options: RNC → SGSN → GGSN → public Internet (the GPRS core)
RNC → MSC → GMSC → public Internet
RNC → GGSN → MSC → Internet
Node B → MSC → SGSN → Internet
questions.explain:
3G runs **two parallel cores** behind the same radio access network (UTRAN = mobile → Node B → **RNC**):
- **Voice:** RNC → **MSC → Gateway MSC** → public telephone network.
- **Data:** RNC → **SGSN → GGSN** → public Internet (GPRS core).
Quote the full component names for the marks: Serving GPRS Support Node, Gateway GPRS Support Node.

questions.prompt: A user on a call moves between base stations under the SAME MSC. This process and its two main triggers are:
options: Handoff — (1) stronger signal from the new BSS, (2) load balancing to free a congested cell
Roaming — (1) billing change, (2) new SIM
Paging — (1) incoming call, (2) SMS
Tunneling — (1) encryption, (2) compression
questions.explain: **Handoff** steps (common MSC): old BSS informs MSC → MSC sets up path to new BSS → new BSS allocates a radio channel → old BSS tells the mobile to switch → mobile + new BSS activate → **MSC reroutes the call** and releases the old resources. The call continues without interruption — that's the design goal.
